results_and_observations: Pathology: Tubular adenomas with low-grade dysplasia; margins clear; no high-grade dysplasia or malignancy
Surveillance guideline recommendation: Repeat colonoscopy in 7 to 10 years

clinical_knowledge.topic: Setting a 7-10 year surveillance interval for two completely resected low-risk tubular adenomas and correcting the fear that polyps 'grow back quickly'
clinical_knowledge.review_status: guideline-grounded sample; clinician review still recommended before release
core_concepts: Post-polypectomy surveillance intervals are risk-stratified by the number, size, and histology of polyps found: one to two small (under 10 mm) tubular adenomas with only low-grade dysplasia is a low-risk finding, and current multisociety guidance supports a long 7-10 year interval before the next colonoscopy — the same interval as an average-risk screening exam.

Tubular adenoma is the most common type of colorectal polyp and represents a precancerous, not cancerous, lesion; complete removal with clear margins (as documented here) removes essentially all of the cancer risk that specific polyp carried.

Low-grade dysplasia describes mild, early cellular changes that carry very low malignant potential compared to high-grade dysplasia, which is a more advanced and higher-risk finding — this pathology report is reassuring specifically because it does not mention high-grade dysplasia.

Diana's next colonoscopy interval will only get shorter than 7-10 years if future findings (more polyps, larger polyps, higher-grade dysplasia, villous histology) put her in a higher-risk category — a favorable first surveillance colonoscopy does not permanently guarantee a long interval forever.
diagnostic_clues: Two polyps, one 6 mm and one 4 mm, both under the 10 mm threshold that would trigger a shorter surveillance interval, supports the low-risk classification.
Tubular histology with only low-grade dysplasia and clear resection margins together confirm complete, curative removal without residual concerning tissue at the excision site.
No high-grade dysplasia or malignancy on pathology is the single most reassuring line in the report and directly addresses her core question about whether this means she has cancer.

An uneventful recovery with no rectal bleeding, severe cramping, fever, or dizziness confirms no post-polypectomy complication (such as delayed bleeding or perforation), which is worth explicitly confirming even though it is expected.
common_misconceptions: Diana's fear that these polyps will 'grow back quickly' conflates the completely removed polyps (which cannot regrow from where they were excised) with the possibility of new, different polyps forming elsewhere over years — which is exactly why long-interval surveillance, not urgent rechecking, is the guideline-recommended approach.

Believing that any polyp found on colonoscopy means cancer was present, when the vast majority of colorectal polyps, including hers, are adenomas that were removed well before any cancer could develop.
Assuming that 'low-grade dysplasia' is a diagnosis of early cancer rather than a description of mild, low-risk cellular change well short of malignancy.

Expecting to need another colonoscopy soon (within a year or two) 'just to be safe,' when unnecessarily frequent colonoscopies carry their own procedural risks without added benefit for someone in her low-risk category.
dangerous_errors: Failing to clearly state the actual recommended interval (7-10 years) and instead leaving her with vague reassurance, which could lead to either unnecessary anxiety or a missed future screening.

Not distinguishing tubular adenoma with low-grade dysplasia from high-grade dysplasia or invasive cancer when explaining the report, which could either underplay or (more commonly, in a worried patient) overplay the seriousness of the finding.
Omitting a review of post-polypectomy red-flag symptoms (delayed bleeding can occur up to two weeks after resection) even though she is currently asymptomatic.

Not confirming her personal and family colorectal cancer history are already accounted for in this interval recommendation, since a strong family history could warrant a different (shorter) surveillance schedule regardless of these particular pathology results.
management_principles: Clearly confirm that this pathology report shows benign, completely removed precancerous polyps with no evidence of cancer.
Explain the specific recommended surveillance interval — 7 to 10 years — and why that interval is appropriate for exactly two small tubular adenomas with low-grade dysplasia.
Directly reassure her that removed polyps do not regrow at the same site; future colonoscopies are looking for any new polyps that may form over time, not a recurrence of these ones.
Document the surveillance plan clearly and give her a specific target year for her next colonoscopy so it is not left as an open-ended 'someday.'
boundaries_and_exceptions: A strong family history of colorectal cancer or a hereditary polyposis syndrome would override this average low-risk interval and require closer surveillance regardless of today's benign pathology.
If a future colonoscopy finds three or more adenomas, any adenoma 10 mm or larger, villous histology, or high-grade dysplasia, the next surveillance interval would shorten substantially.

New symptoms before the next scheduled colonoscopy — rectal bleeding, unexplained weight loss, or a significant change in bowel habits — would warrant earlier evaluation regardless of the surveillance schedule.
